image_description: The image displays two sea lions resting on a wooden dock structure near water. The primary subject is a large, dark-colored male sea lion in the foreground, characterized by a prominent sagittal crest and thick neck mane. A second, lighter-colored sea lion (likely female or juvenile) is visible behind it to the left. Both animals exhibit wet, sleek fur typical of pinnipeds.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Head is broad with prominent sagittal crest in males.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The foreground subject clearly displays the characteristic bony bump (sagittal crest) on the top of its head, consistent with an adult male sea lion.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: External ear pinnae (visible ear flaps) distinguish from true seals.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Small but distinct external ear flaps are visible on the side of the head of the foreground animal, confirming it is an otariid (sea lion/fur seal) rather than a phocid (true seal).
Stiff, light-colored whiskers are clearly visible protruding from the muzzle area of both animals.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Fur is short and coarse ranging from brown to dark grey, lighter on ventral surface.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The fur appears short and sleek (wet look). The foreground male is dark brown/black, while the background animal is lighter tan/brown, fitting the color variation description.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body exhibits streamlined fusiform form of substantial marine mammal proportions.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The body shape is robust, tapered, and streamlined, consistent with a large marine mammal adapted for swimming.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Males develop thick neck mane and are significantly larger than females.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The foreground animal shows a thickening of the skin/fur around the neck (mane) and appears physically larger and darker than the companion behind it, indicating sexual dimorphism.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Foreflippers are large, broad, and hairless on underside used for terrestrial locomotion.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The foreflippers are largely occluded by the animal's body position and the angle of the shot; the underside texture cannot be verified.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Hind flippers can rotate forward for walking on land.

Despite the pose, the visible anatomical landmarks (eyes, ears, nostrils) align symmetrically along the central axis of the head and body.
